title: Hosted API Demo - Chat/Text Generation Basics
summary: AE+SE walkthrough of Redwood hosted API focusing on chat and text generation primitives: streaming responses, parameters (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), retry behavior and idempotency, and integration patterns. Customer asked about latency/cost tradeoffs, VPC/private options, SOC2 and data retention. Agreed next steps: share pricing sheet, security docs, and run a short bench (3k messages) with sample prompts.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45 min
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Maya (Solara Eng), Liam (Solara CTO), Priya (Solara Security)

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Samir and Jordan on the engineering side. Can you hear us ok?
00:08 Maya: Yep, all good here, thanks.
00:12 Alex: Cool quick agenda — we'll do a 25 minute demo of hosted API for chat/text generation, cover streaming, parameters and retries, then leave time for Q&A and next steps.
00:22 Liam: Sounds good, timeline wise we're looking to pilot next quarter, wanted to understand performance and security first.
00:30 Samir: Great, to kick off — can you share a little about your stack so we can focus the demo? Are you running in AWS? Any VPC/airgap needs?
00:38 Maya: We're AWS, multi-account. No on-prem for phase 1. We do have strict data retention and need SOC 2 type controls. Priya will chime in on security.
00:47 Priya: Yeah SOC 2 is a baseline, and we need audit logs and KMS integration for keys. Also curious around log retention and who can see raw prompts.
00:56 Alex: Totally. Redwood hosted keeps control plane logs for X days (we'll share exact retention in the security pack). You can opt for encrypted-at-rest with customer KMS for Private deployments; hosted has a defined retention and redaction options. We'll attach docs.
01:10 Samir: Ok jumping into the API — show of hands who has used LLM APIs before? (pause) good. We'll demo two modes: non-streaming batch text generation and streaming chat, show how streaming reduces tail latency and how to handle retries.
01:28 Samir: (share screen) This is a quick curl and SDK example. Example request: model: redwood-alpha-1, messages: array, max_tokens 256, temperature 0.2. Using the streaming flag you get chunked tokens as SSE/websocket like events.
01:45 Maya: Is streaming implemented as server-sent events? Any websocket option?
01:49 Samir: Right now hosted supports SSE-style streaming over the same endpoint; SDKs handle assembling partials. We also have a websocket preview in private deploys for lower latency but SSE covers most use cases.
02:05 Jordan: Note: sometimes the transcript from our research is imperfect — a lot of customers call it stream socket — it's SSE.
02:14 Maya: Got it. How frequently do chunks arrive? Do you buffer at token boundaries?
02:20 Samir: Chunks are emitted roughly every 50-200ms depending on model and token emission. We send token deltas; SDKs can give partial content rapidly. For long form you see progressive rendering.
02:35 Liam: What's the expected average latency per token? Say for 20 tokens?
02:40 Samir: For common models on hosted, first token often <100ms on our faster tiers; per-token thereafter ~10-30ms. Real numbers depend on model size and sequence length. We'll provide benchmark sheets.
02:55 Priya: Any jitter concerns? We need consistent performance for UX SLAs.
02:59 Samir: We have latency SLOs on dedicated tiers; hosted has best-effort but we measure percentiles and surface them in the Console. Also automatic fallback to smaller model variants if needed.
03:14 Alex: Now parameters — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and presence/penalty plumb into requests. Quick demo: raise temperature to 0.8 for creative tone.
03:29 Alex: Watch the output change. (shows examples) Also you can set streaming:true and read partials while the model continues.
03:41 Maya: If the client disconnects mid-stream what happens? Do you need a retry or resume token?
03:46 Samir: Good Q. If disconnected, the request is aborted server-side. We recommend idempotency keys for retriable requests. For chat where you care about full context you can re-issue with the same messages and idempotency key; our servers dedupe replays for a short window. There's no stream-resume token yet.
04:05 Maya: Ok. How do retries work — exponential backoff, idempotency?
04:09 Samir: We suggest a retry policy: 3 attempts max, exponential backoff starting at 200ms, and use idempotency keys for operations that mustn't double-charge. For streaming we detect partial output; we recommend client-side merging with server dedupe if needed.
04:23 Jordan: Small note — some customers call the idempotency param request_id or idempotency_key; our SDK exposes idempotencyKey.
04:30 Liam: Pricing — can you give a sense how streaming affects billing?
04:34 Alex: Billing is still per-token; streaming doesn't change cost, it's just transport. Cost depends on input + output tokens. We also have tiered pricing and committed capacity for lower unit costs.
04:46 Maya: Any caching to reduce cost? We have repetitive prompts for summarization.
04:51 Samir: We support prefix and KV caching in the runtime, and recommend deterministic prompt templates for cacheability; we can show Optimize suggestions to identify cacheable patterns.
05:02 Priya: About data retention — will raw prompts be stored on hosted? For how long?
05:07 Alex: Hosted stores transient logs for X days for monitoring; we can redact and offer minimal retention for compliance. For full control use Redwood Private. We'll attach SOC2 and data retention specifics.
05:20 Maya: Ok can you show a quick code example with the JS SDK?
05:24 Samir: Sure. (shows code) const client = new RedwoodClient({apiKey: process.env.RW_API_KEY}); const stream = await client.chat.stream({model: 'redwood-alpha-1', messages: [...], max_tokens: 200, temperature: 0.2}); stream.on('data', chunk => { render(chunk.text) });
05:43 Maya: Nice. Does the SDK reassemble tokens automatically?
05:46 Samir: Yes the SDK emits assembled deltas and final messages; low-level events give token-by-token if you need.
05:54 Jordan: Another practical thing — concurrency and rate limits. Hosted APIs have per-account rate limits; we throttle with 429s and include Retry-After headers. For high throughput we recommend Dedicated.
06:09 Liam: How is burst handled? We have uneven traffic.
06:12 Samir: We offer burst credits on Dedicated and configurable autoscaling. Hosted can handle typical PLG bursts but Dedicated is for predictable throughput.
06:21 Maya: A lot of our latency is from tokenization and long context windows, how does Redwood handle long contexts?
06:26 Samir: We do KV cache management and chunking; for very long contexts we recommend strategies like relevance re-ranking and rolling context windows. Also quantization and kernel selection help performance for private/dedicated.
06:40 Priya: For security integrations — SSO, SAML, RBAC?
06:44 Alex: Hosted supports SAML SSO at org-level and RBAC for API keys; audit logs available. For stricter needs Private gives VPC and KMS.
06:54 Maya: We might need VPC egress restrictions if we do pilot. Is there an IP allowlist?
06:58 Alex: Yes hosted supports IP allowlisting for orgs, and we can do private peering for Dedicated or Private.
07:06 Liam: Ok let's go back to streaming specifics — any guidance for client-side UI rendering to avoid jank?
07:12 Samir: Render partials incrementally but debounce UI updates to ~50ms, assemble tokens into words to avoid mid-word flashes. SDKs provide word-boundary helpers.
07:24 Maya: On retries, is there a way to detect duplicate outputs if the model returns the same text on retry?
07:31 Samir: Dedupe on server with idempotency keys; client can also attach a request fingerprint. Non-idempotent operations (like charging an external API) should be protected client-side.
07:44 Jordan: Quick demo of a failed request and retry flow — (shows 500, then retry with backoff).
07:54 Maya: I noticed in the example you passed system prompt and user messages — how do you recommend structuring messages for multi-turn?
07:59 Samir: Keep system for behavior, then array of user/assistant messages. For very long histories we suggest summarizing prior turns into a condensed memory message to keep context window small.
08:14 Liam: Any client libraries in python? We prefer python for backend.
08:18 Alex: Yes python, node, and a simple curl endpoint. We'll share code snippets.
08:23 Maya: For the bench, we'd like to run 3k messages across 3 templates with 95th percentile latency under 500ms. Feasible?
08:32 Samir: On our faster hosted tier and small/medium models that is feasible; we'll propose a bench plan. If you need <200ms stable, Dedicated is better.
08:42 Priya: Are there data residency options for EU?
08:46 Alex: Yes region controls and EU data residency in certain regions; Private is full control.
08:51 Speaker 1: [inaudible]
08:53 Jordan: Some transcription glitches earlier — couple acronyms get mangled like KV cash for KV cache in auto-transcripts.
09:00 Maya: That's fine.
09:02 Samir: Wrapping to retries — also make sure to capture partial outputs in your UI in case of retries so you can resume gracefully.
09:11 Alex: Ok let's do a short live prompt demo — we'll run a summarization prompt streaming so you can see partials. (runs example)
09:25 Samir: Streaming partial 1: "In Q1 we shipped..." partial 2: "The new auth flow reduced..." final assembled: "In Q1 we shipped the new auth flow which reduced..."
09:46 Maya: Looks good. Any rate-limit headers to look for?
09:50 Jordan: 429 + Retry-After; we also include X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.
09:55 Liam: How do we instrument cost-per-session?
10:00 Alex: Console shows token-level breakdown, per-route cost, and you can tag requests. We also export to BigQuery.
10:10 Maya: Can we get a CSV for cost on recent usage?
10:13 Alex: Yes we'll include a sample and the Console export settings.
10:18 Priya: For security review we'll need SOC2 report and the endpoint of contact.
10:22 Alex: We'll attach security pack and schedule a follow-up with our Security SE.
10:27 Jordan: Quick note on model rollouts — you can pin model versions or set split rollouts for canary. If new model regresses we have automatic fallback to previous variant.
10:40 Liam: Any competitor comparisons? We've looked at other managed APIs.
10:44 Alex: Common names we hear are OpenAI, Anthropic, and some infra vendors like Replicate for self-hosting. We can share performance comparisons we did on standard prompts.
10:56 Maya: Let's talk integration timeline — if we start pilot in April, what's realistic?
11:01 Alex: A two-week integration then bench week then review is common. With your team size we can aim for mid-April pilot start.
11:10 Samir: Last demo bit — retries + streaming edge-case: if a retry returns additional tokens the SDK will flag a partialThenFinal event so you can reconcile.
11:22 Maya: Nice. For the bench we need sample model ids and recommended settings.
11:27 Samir: We'll propose a plan: model small-medium, temperature 0.2, max_tokens 150, streaming true for UI flows. We'll deliver a script.
11:36 Alex: Great. Any other questions?
11:39 Priya: One more on logs — can we plug logs into Splunk?
11:42 Alex: Yes export to S3 or SIEM integrations; we'll include details.
11:48 Liam: Ok that's helpful.
11:51 Alex: We'll recap next steps now.
12:00 Alex: Thanks everyone — end of demo.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-attributions and auto-transcript garbling present (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache, "salmo" for SAML), timestamps approximate.
